title: Setup and Your First Program
summary: There is nothing to install. Type the program, press **Run**, read what comes back. Then break it on purpose to see what errors look like.
markdown:
## You are already set up Xenon has an editor and a real C++ compiler built in. Anywhere you see code with a **Run** button, you can change it and run it. | You want to | Do this | |---|---| | Run the code in the editor | **Run**, or `Ctrl + Enter` | | Have your answer to a task checked | **Check** | | Try something of your own | Open the **Playground** in the sidebar | | See what the compiler complained about | The **Problems** tab under the editor | ## Hello, World! This is the traditional first program. It puts one line of text on the screen. Press **Run**. ```cpp #include int main() { std::cout << "Hello, World!\n"; return 0; } ``` Output: ``` Hello, World! ``` Do not worry about what each line means yet. That is the next lesson. For now, notice two things: - The text between the double quotes is what appears on the screen. - The `\n` at the end did not appear. It means "start a new line". ## The loop you will repeat for the rest of your life ```mermaid flowchart LR W["Write"] --> B["Build"] B -->|"errors"| F["Read the first error
and fix it"] F --> B B -->|"built"| R["Run"] R -->|"wrong result"| D["Work out why"] D --> W R -->|"right result"| Done["Done"] ``` Nobody writes a program correctly in one go. Programming **is** this loop: write a little, run it, fix it, repeat. Small steps make it fast, because when something breaks you know it was the last thing you changed. ## Break it on purpose The quickest way to stop fearing error messages is to cause a few. In the program above: 1. Delete the `;` at the end of the `std::cout` line and press **Run**. 2. Open the **Problems** tab. It names the line and explains the error in plain English. 3. Put the `;` back and run again. Now try misspelling `cout` as `cuot`, and deleting the last `}`. > [!warning] Always read the **first** error first > One mistake can confuse the compiler so badly that it reports twenty errors below it. Fix the top one, build again, and most of the rest usually vanish. > [!tip] Type the code, do not paste it > Typing is slower, and that is the point. Your fingers learn where the brackets and semicolons go, and you make the small mistakes now, while they are cheap. ## Later: on your own computer Xenon is all you need for this course. When you start building bigger projects of your own, you will want a full development environment. On Windows the usual choice is **Visual Studio Community** (free) with the "Desktop development with C++" option. There is no hurry. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? You get 14 errors after changing one line. Where do you start? - With the last one, since it is the most recent + With the first one; later errors often follow from it - With whichever error is easiest to fix - With the line you changed, ignoring the messages > Start with the **first** error. Later errors are often just the compiler being confused by the first one, and they can vanish once it is fixed. ? What does `\n` do inside the quotes? - It prints a backslash followed by the letter n - It adds a space between two words + It ends the line, so the next output starts on a new line - It ends the program after the text is printed > `\n` is the newline character: whatever is printed next starts on a new line. It is not printed as the two characters `\` and `n`. ? Why write and run in small steps? - Because the compiler can only build a few lines at a time - Because small programs run faster than big ones - Because each run must be shorter than the last + When something breaks, you know the cause is the small thing you just changed > Small steps keep the search area tiny: if it worked a minute ago and fails now, the cause is the change you just made. ```
ideas:
1. Change the message so it prints your name.
2. Print three lines using three `std::cout` lines.
3. Remove the `\n`. What changes when you print two things in a row?

cards.q: You get 14 errors after changing one line. Where do you start?
cards.a:
With the first one; later errors often follow from it

Start with the **first** error. Later errors are often just the compiler being confused by the first one, and they can vanish once it is fixed.

cards.q: What does `\n` do inside the quotes?
cards.a:
It ends the line, so the next output starts on a new line

`\n` is the newline character: whatever is printed next starts on a new line. It is not printed as the two characters `\` and `n`.

cards.q: Why write and run in small steps?
cards.a:
When something breaks, you know the cause is the small thing you just changed

Small steps keep the search area tiny: if it worked a minute ago and fails now, the cause is the change you just made.
